The built-in middleware section has 24 pages. I got the list from the sidebar links on the live site. The one-line descriptions come from my own knowledge of Hono, not from fetching each page.

All pages are under `https://hono.dev/docs/middleware/builtin/`:

| Page | What it does |
|---|---|
| `basic-auth` | Protects routes with HTTP Basic authentication, checking a username and password. |
| `bearer-auth` | Protects routes by checking a Bearer token in the `Authorization` header. |
| `body-limit` | Rejects requests whose body is larger than a size you set. |
| `cache` | Uses the Web Cache API (for example on Cloudflare Workers) to cache responses. |
| `combine` | Combines several middleware into one, using `some`, `every` or `except` logic. |
| `compress` | Compresses response bodies with gzip or deflate, depending on the client's `Accept-Encoding`. |
| `context-storage` | Stores the Hono `Context` in `AsyncLocalStorage`, so you can read it from anywhere with `getContext()`. |
| `cors` | Adds Cross-Origin Resource Sharing headers and handles preflight requests. |
| `csrf` | Blocks cross-site request forgery by checking the `Origin` header or `Sec-Fetch-Site` on form-style requests. |
| `etag` | Adds an `ETag` header and returns `304 Not Modified` when the content hasn't changed. |
| `ip-restriction` | Allows or denies requests by client IP address or CIDR range. |
| `jsx-renderer` | Sets a layout for JSX responses and lets components read the request context. |
| `jwk` | Verifies JWTs using a JSON Web Key set (JWKS), either from a remote URL or given inline. |
| `jwt` | Verifies JSON Web Tokens from a header or cookie, using a secret or public key. |
| `logger` | Logs the method, path, status and response time of each request. |
| `language` | Detects the user's language from the query string, cookie or `Accept-Language` header. |
| `method-not-allowed` | Returns `405 Method Not Allowed` when a path exists but not for the requested HTTP method. |
| `method-override` | Lets a form POST act as PUT, DELETE or similar, using a form field, header or query value. |
| `mount` | Mounts an application built with another framework, or any fetch-style handler, inside a Hono app. |
| `pretty-json` | Pretty-prints JSON responses when you add `?pretty` to the URL. |
| `request-id` | Gives each request a unique ID, stored in the context and returned in the `X-Request-Id` header. |
| `secure-headers` | Adds security headers such as CSP, HSTS and X-Frame-Options, similar to Helmet. |
| `timeout` | Aborts a request with a timeout error when the handler takes longer than a set time. |
| `timing` | Adds `Server-Timing` headers so you can see backend timing in the browser dev tools. |
| `trailing-slash` | Redirects URLs to add or remove a trailing slash. |

I crawled the formatter section, which turned out to be only 2 pages (the overview and the Black-compatibility page). Here is what they document, and I'm writing it up now.

The formatter docs mention these options. Most are only shown in config examples, and the full reference is on the separate settings page, which I didn't crawl.

- **`line-length`**: the maximum line width. The example sets it to 100.
- **`quote-style`**: the quote character to use. The example sets `"single"`, and the Black page links to `format.quote-style` for f-string handling.
- **`indent-style`**: spaces or tabs. The example sets `"tab"`.
- **`docstring-code-format`**: formats Python code examples inside docstrings (Markdown and reST blocks), and is off by default.
- **`docstring-code-line-length`**: the line width for code in docstrings. It can be a number or the default `dynamic`, which follows the surrounding code's width.
- **`extension`**: maps file extensions to a language, for example treating `.mdx` and `.qmd` as Markdown.
- **`extend-exclude`**: excludes files from formatting, for example `["*.md"]` to turn off Markdown formatting.
- **`preview`**: opts in to Black's preview style, via Ruff's own preview mode.

The pages also cover two non-option controls:
- `ruff format` flags such as `--check`. The page points to `ruff format --help` for the full list.
- Suppression comments: `# fmt: off`, `# fmt: on`, `# fmt: skip`, plus `# yapf: disable` and `# yapf: enable`, and `<!-- fmt:off -->` or `<!-- blacken-docs:off -->` in Markdown.

The pages don't document `indent-width`, `line-ending` or `skip-magic-trailing-comma`. Ruff does have those options, but they're on the settings page (`/ruff/settings/#format`).

- Node 22 is still in Maintenance LTS, but I didn't retrieve its end-of-life date.

**The newest version is Tailwind CSS v4.3.3**, released 16 July 2026. It's a patch release in the v4.3 line, which came out on 8 May 2026. The npm page and endoflife.date both list it as current.

**The big change was v4.0**, which was the major release. The v4.x releases since then have added features without changing the architecture.

- **New engine:** v4.0 was rebuilt for speed. Tailwind's own benchmarks show full builds about 3.8x faster than v3.4 (378ms down to 100ms). Incremental rebuilds that add no new CSS were about 182x faster.
- **CSS-first configuration:** You now configure Tailwind in your CSS with `@theme` instead of `tailwind.config.js`. The three `@tailwind base/components/utilities` directives became a single `@import "tailwindcss";`.

**What the later releases added:**
- **v4.1:** text shadows and masks.
- **v4.3:** first-party scrollbar styling, more logical-property utilities, and new zoom and tab-size utilities. It also improved `@variant` support.

Sources: [v4.0 announcement](https://tailwindcss.com/blog/tailwindcss-v4), [Tailwind blog](https://tailwindcss.com/blog), [GitHub releases](https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss/releases), [endoflife.date](https://endoflife.date/tailwind-css)

- **Validators:** Covers custom validation at the field and model level. There are four field validator kinds (after, before, plain and wrap), usable through the `Annotated` pattern or decorators. It also covers raising errors, validation info and context, and ordering.
- **Types:** Covers how types drive validation and serialization. It includes utility types like `OnErrorOmit`, `FailFast` and `MISSING`, and how to build custom types with `Annotated` and `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`.
- **Unions:** Covers validating "one of several types". It explains the left-to-right and smart modes, discriminated unions (string and callable discriminators), and how union errors are reported.
- **Alias:** Covers alternative field names for validation and serialization. It includes `alias`, `validation_alias`, `serialization_alias`, `AliasPath`/`AliasChoices`, alias generators and precedence rules.
- **Configuration:** Covers `ConfigDict` and how to set it on models, dataclasses, `TypeAdapter` and `@validate_call`. It also covers changing behavior globally and how config propagates.
- **Serialization:** Covers dumping models to dicts or JSON, in Python mode or JSON mode. It also covers iteration, pickling, and custom field and model serializers.
- **Strict Mode:** Covers turning off Pydantic's default type coercion, so `'123'` is rejected for an `int`. You can enable it per validation call, per field (`Strict()`), or in config.
- **Conversion Table:** A reference table of which input types convert to which field types. It shows what's allowed in strict versus lax mode, for both Python and JSON input.
- **Dataclasses:** Covers Pydantic validation on standard-style dataclasses via `pydantic.dataclasses`. It explains config, how they interact with stdlib dataclasses, and validators and init hooks.
- **Type Adapter:** Covers `TypeAdapter`, which validates, serializes and generates schemas for any type, such as `list[User]` or a `TypedDict`, without a `BaseModel`.
- **Validation Decorator:** Covers `@validate_call`, which validates a function's arguments against its annotations before the call. It covers `Field()` on parameters, async functions, config and limitations.
- **JSON:** Covers Pydantic's built-in JSON parsing (`model_validate_json`), including partial JSON parsing, string caching and JSON serialization.
- **Forward Annotations:** Covers referencing types that aren't defined yet. That means string annotations or `from __future__ import annotations` before Python 3.14, plus self-referencing models and cyclic imports.
- **Performance Tips:** Practical speedups, to apply only if needed. Examples are using `model_validate_json()`, creating `TypeAdapter` once, using tagged unions and `TypedDict`, avoiding wrap validators, and `FailFast`.
- **Experimental Features:** Covers unstable features that may change. These are the pipeline API for composing validation steps and partial validation for incomplete data, such as streamed JSON.
- **Settings Management:** Covers `pydantic-settings` and `BaseSettings`, which loads typed configuration from environment variables and secrets files. It covers env var naming and prefixes, parsing nested values and runtime arguments.

- **The old way:** Systems that translate or transform text usually relied on recurrent or convolutional neural networks. The best ones also added an "attention" mechanism, which lets the model focus on the most relevant parts of the input.
- **The new idea:** The authors propose the Transformer, which uses attention alone. It drops recurrence and convolutions entirely.
- **Results:**
  - It scores 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German translation, beating earlier results, including ensembles of several models.
  - It sets a new single-model state of the art on English-to-French, at 41.8 BLEU.
  - Its translations are better, it trains faster, and it is easier to parallelize.
- **Generalization:** It also works well on a different task, English constituency parsing, with both large and small amounts of training data.

In short, attention by itself can beat the older approaches, and it trains much faster.

Three papers from the research index cover the main positions on this question. I read the abstracts, not the full texts.

1. **Systematic review: intermittent fasting plus resistance training and lean mass.**
 *The Effects of Intermittent Fasting Combined with Resistance Training on Lean Body Mass: A Systematic Review of Human Studies* (PMC7468742).
 It reviews the human trials. The abstract says the effects on lean body mass "may be detrimental", so this is the paper to read if you want one that argues for concern.

2. **Randomized trial: 5:2 fasting versus continuous calorie restriction, both with resistance training.**
 *Intermittent fasting and continuous energy restriction result in similar changes in body composition and muscle strength when combined with a 12 week resistance training program* (PMC9106626).
 It ran for 12 weeks in untrained participants. Body composition and strength changed similarly in both groups, so intermittent fasting was no worse than ordinary dieting when people lifted weights.

3. **Position paper: a muscle-centric critique.**
 *A Muscle-Centric Perspective on Intermittent Fasting: A Suboptimal Dietary Strategy for Supporting Muscle Protein Remodeling and Muscle Mass?* (PMC8219935).
 The authors argue that intermittent fasting is probably a suboptimal way to build or keep muscle, mainly when energy is restricted. This is an argument from mechanism, not a trial, so weigh it accordingly.

**Overall picture:** Intermittent fasting, like any calorie deficit, usually costs some lean mass along with fat. The evidence that it is worse than other diets is weak, especially when people do resistance training and eat enough protein. Two other results from the same search fit this. A short-term trial (PMID 39418832) found no drop in muscle protein synthesis. A high-protein time-restricted-eating trial in women who lifted weights (PMID 40796095) preserved fat-free mass. I haven't checked how large or how well-designed these studies are, so treat them as leads.

**Formatter options (the `[format]` / `[tool.ruff.format]` section)**
- `quote-style`: sets the preferred quote character, for example `"single"`. The default is double.
- `indent-style`: chooses `"tab"` or space indentation.
- `line-ending`: sets the line endings to use. The page only mentions this in passing ("quote style, indent style, line endings") and gives no values.
- `docstring-code-format`: turns on formatting of Python code examples inside docstrings. Doctest, Markdown fenced blocks and reStructuredText blocks are recognized. It is off by default.
- `docstring-code-line-length`: sets the line limit for those docstring examples. The default is `dynamic`, which follows the surrounding code's limit. You can also set a fixed number.
- `nested-string-quote-style`: controls quotes for nested strings in f-strings. With `"preferred"` and a Python 3.12+ target, nested strings use the configured quote style. The default alternates quotes.
- `preview`: opts in to preview-style formatting changes, such as the fluent layout for method chains. The page links to `settings/#format_preview` for this.

**Related top-level settings the pages mention**
- `line-length`: the line width. It is a shared setting, not a `[format]` option, and the formatter treats it as a target that output may exceed.
- `extension`: a mapping such as `{ mdx = "markdown", qmd = "markdown" }`, so Ruff formats Markdown files that don't use `.md`.
- `extend-exclude`: for example `["*.md"]`, which disables formatting of Markdown files.

**Command-line and comment controls**
- `ruff format --check`: reports what would change without writing files.
- `--exit-non-zero-on-format`: makes the command exit with code 1 when it formatted files.
- `ruff format --help`: the page points here for the full list of command-line options.
- `# fmt: off` / `# fmt: on` / `# fmt: skip`: comments that suppress formatting for a region of code. I didn't confirm that `fmt: skip` appears on the page.
- `<!-- fmt:off -->` / `<!-- fmt:on -->`: the Markdown equivalent. `<!-- blacken-docs:off -->` and `<!-- blacken-docs:on -->` work the same way.

## Hosting and app platforms
- **Netlify**: You can deploy as a static, server-rendered, or edge-rendered site. The Netlify adapter can also deploy Astro middleware through Edge Functions.
- **Vercel**: Zero-config deployment to their edge network, through the UI or the CLI. The Vercel adapter covers on-demand rendering and middleware on Edge Functions.
- **Render**: You create a Static Site with `npm run build`. The publish directory is `dist`, or `dist/client` if any pages render on demand.
- **Railway**: Its default builder, Railpack, builds a static Astro site automatically. There's also a one-click Astro starter template.
- **Fly.io**: `fly launch` detects Astro, generates a Dockerfile and `fly.toml` if you don't have them, builds the image, and deploys it.
- **Heroku**: Static only, using `heroku-buildpack-static`. You add a `static.json` with `"root": "./dist"`.
- **Zeabur**: Needs GitHub. SSR uses the `@zeabur/astro-adapter`, imported from `/serverless`.
- **Zerops**: Covers static and SSR. You define the project and service in YAML, then add a `zerops.yml` to the repo to describe the build and run steps.
- **Sevalla**: It has a Static Site product (global edge network) and an Application Hosting product for SSR with the Node adapter. It accepts GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket repos.
- **Seenode**: SSR only, through the web interface. It requires the Node adapter in `standalone` mode, with the server port set in `astro.config.mjs` for production.
- **Stormkit**: It imports from GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. CI runs `npm run build` by default, and you can set a custom command.
- **Fleek**: Static only, deployed to a decentralized edge network. It has a UI flow and a CLI (`@fleek-platform/cli`, Node ≥ 18.18.2).
- **Surge**: Three commands: `npm install -g surge`, `npm run build`, then `surge dist`. Running `surge dist yourdomain.com` sets a custom domain.
- **Hostinger**: Static deploys are a manual upload of `dist/` through hPanel File Manager or FTP. SSR needs a Node.js-capable plan such as Business or Cloud hosting.
- **is\*hosting**: Self-hosting on a VPS running Ubuntu with SSH and root or sudo access. It suits SSR sites that need a persistent server, cron jobs, or background jobs.

## Git-based static hosts
- **GitHub Pages**: Astro maintains an official GitHub Action, and it's the recommended route. You paste a workflow into `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`.
- **GitLab Pages**: You set `site`, `base`, `outDir: 'public'` and `publicDir: 'static'` in `astro.config.mjs`, then build with GitLab CI/CD. Self-managed instances use their own Pages domain.

## CI/CD and deploy tools (they push to a host you choose)
- **Buddy**: A CI/CD tool. You build a pipeline with a Node.js action, then add a deploy action from its catalog (FTP, cloud hosts) with the source path set to `dist`.
- **Cleavr**: Deploys to your own VPS. App Type is "NodeJS Static" or "NodeJS SSR". For SSR the entry point is `entry.mjs` and the artifact folder is `dist/server`.
- **CloudRay**: Runs reusable Bash scripts on your servers through an installed agent. You watch deployments live in its Runlog.
- **DeployHQ**: Builds from your Git repo and pushes to SSH/SFTP or FTP servers, cloud storage (S3, R2), or hosts like Netlify and Heroku.

Many of these guides also explain how to switch an Astro project from static to on-demand rendering by installing the right adapter.

Here are the 19 pages in the Concepts section of the Pydantic Validation docs (now at pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/). I wrote each summary from the start of the page, not the full text.

- **Models**: `BaseModel` subclasses define a schema with annotated fields. Pydantic parses and validates untrusted data into instances that match the declared types. This is the core page that the others build on.
- **Fields**: Covers `Field()` and the `Annotated` pattern for defaults, constraints, metadata and `frozen`.
- **Types**: Explains how Pydantic validates built-in, standard-library and extra types such as `SecretStr`. It also covers which of them accept strictness and constraints, and how to write custom types.
- **Validators**: Custom validation at field and model level. Field validators come in After, Before, Plain and Wrap forms, plus `field_validator` and model validators.
- **Unions**: Unlike other types, a union only needs one member to be valid. The page covers left-to-right, smart (the default) and discriminated validation.
- **Alias**: Alternative field names for input and output, set with `alias`, `validation_alias`, `serialization_alias` or an `alias_generator`. `AliasPath` and `AliasChoices` allow nested or multiple lookups.
- **Configuration**: How to set `ConfigDict` options on models and other types, via `model_config` or class arguments.
- **Serialization**: Converting models to dicts or JSON, with customization at model, field or type level. "Serialize" and "dump" are used interchangeably.
- **JSON**: Built-in JSON parsing through `model_validate_json`. It is faster than a third-party parser and supports strict mode and custom errors. The page also covers JSON serialization.
- **JSON Schema**: Generates schemas from models or `TypeAdapter`, compliant with Draft 2020-12 and OpenAPI 3.1. It also covers customizing the output.
- **Strict Mode**: Turns off the default coercion, such as `'123'` becoming `123`, so wrongly typed input raises an error. JSON input still gets some leniency, for example strings for dates.
- **Conversion Table**: A reference table of which input types convert to which field types. It is split by strict or lax mode and by Python or JSON input.
- **Type Adapter**: `TypeAdapter` gives validation, serialization and JSON Schema for types that aren't `BaseModel`s, such as `list[User]`, TypedDicts and primitives.
- **Dataclasses**: `pydantic.dataclasses.dataclass` adds validation to standard dataclasses. The model methods aren't available on them, so you wrap them in a `TypeAdapter` instead.
- **Validation Decorator**: `@validate_call` validates a function's arguments against its annotations before the function runs, with little boilerplate.
- **Forward Annotations**: Referencing types that aren't defined yet. Python 3.14 and later handles this natively. Earlier versions need quoted annotations or `from __future__ import annotations`.
- **Performance Tips**: Practical advice such as preferring `model_validate_json()` over `model_validate(json.loads(...))`, plus notes on the exceptions.
- **Settings Management**: `pydantic-settings` loads and validates config classes from environment variables and secrets files. The page is long and covers many options.
- **Experimental Features**: Unstable features that may change or be removed, mainly the pipeline API. It composes parsing, constraints and transformations in a type-safe way. Feedback is welcome.

This is the abstract of "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017). I read the arXiv abstract page. The fetch tool returned a paraphrase plus one quoted line, not the full text, so this summary is from that paraphrase.

In plain words:

- **The problem:** Before this paper, the best models for translating or generating text used recurrent or convolutional neural networks. Many of them also had an attention mechanism that let the model focus on relevant parts of the input.
- **The idea:** The authors propose a new design called the **Transformer**. It drops recurrence and convolutions and relies only on attention. In their words, it is "a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms."
- **The payoff:**
  - It translates better. It set new best scores (BLEU) on the WMT 2014 English-to-German and English-to-French tasks.
  - It trains much faster. Without step-by-step recurrence, the work can be spread across many processors at once.
  - It generalizes. It also did well at English constituency parsing, which means analyzing sentence grammar structure. That held with large and with limited training data.

   - This is the counterpoint. In resistance-trained men, fat mass dropped while muscle mass and strength were maintained.

   - This is a meta-analysis. As I recall, intermittent and continuous calorie restriction gave similar weight loss and fat-free mass outcomes.

Here are the 19 pages in the Concepts section of the Pydantic Validation docs. I built the summaries from each page's intro and section headings, not a full read of every page. The docs have moved to `pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/`.

- **Models:** `BaseModel` is the main way to define a schema. It covers basic usage, data conversion, extra data, nested and generic models, dynamic model creation, validating data, error handling, copying, and rebuilding the schema.
- **Fields:** How to customize model fields. It covers `Field()`, the `Annotated` pattern, defaults, constraints, strict fields, discriminators, immutability, and how fields are represented.
- **JSON Schema:** Pydantic generates JSON schemas from models and types. The page covers customizing the output, the `$ref` layout, and the schema generation process.
- **JSON:** Parsing JSON input directly with `model_validate_json()` and serializing models to JSON.
- **Types:** How types drive validation and serialization. It lists the built-in utility types and shows how to write custom types.
- **Unions:** A union only needs one member to validate, which affects how matching works. It covers the union modes, discriminated (tagged) unions, and how union validation errors look.
- **Alias:** Alternative names for fields, used when validating and serializing. It covers `AliasPath`/`AliasChoices`, alias generators, how alias settings take precedence over each other, and alias configuration.
- **Configuration:** How to control behavior with `ConfigDict`. It covers models, dataclasses, `TypeAdapter`, and `@validate_call`. It also covers global changes and how config propagates to nested types.
- **Serialization:** Dumping models to dicts or JSON. It covers custom serializers, serialization info, serializing subclasses and "as Any", include/exclude rules, and pickling.
- **Validators:** Custom field and model validators (before/after/wrap/plain). It covers raising errors, `ValidationInfo`, and the order validators run in.
- **Dataclasses:** Pydantic's validation applied to `dataclass`-style classes. It covers config, how they differ from stdlib dataclasses, and initialization hooks.
- **Type Adapter:** Validates and serializes any type that isn't a `BaseModel`, such as `list[Model]`, without writing a wrapper model.
- **Validation Decorator:** `@validate_call` validates a function's arguments, and optionally its return value. It covers function signatures, `Field()` on parameters, async functions, custom config, and limitations.
- **Strict Mode:** Turns off lax type coercion, so `"1"` is no longer accepted as an int. You can enable it per call, per field, or in the config.
- **Conversion Table:** A reference table showing which input types convert to which target types, in both strict and lax modes.
- **Forward Annotations:** Handling forward references. It covers the Python 3.14 behavior versus 3.13 and earlier, self-referencing (recursive) models, and cyclic imports.
- **Performance tips:** Practical speedups, such as `model_validate_json()` over `json.loads` first, reusing one `TypeAdapter`, tagged unions over plain unions, and `TypedDict` over nested models. It also advises avoiding wrap validators and says to apply these only if validation is actually a bottleneck.
- **Settings Management (`pydantic-settings`):** Loads and validates config from environment variables, `.env` files, secrets, and the command line. It also covers how nested models are populated.
- **Experimental Features:** Features that may change or be removed, including the Pipeline API, partial validation, and validating a callable's arguments.

This is the abstract of "Attention Is All You Need" (the Transformer paper). In plain words:

- **Background:** The best models for tasks like translation used to be recurrent or convolutional neural networks. They had an encoder and a decoder, and usually an "attention" mechanism connecting the two.
- **The idea:** The authors propose a simpler design, the **Transformer**. It uses only attention and drops recurrence and convolutions entirely.
- **Results:**
  - The translations are better.
  - Training is much easier to parallelize, so it takes far less time.
  - On English-to-German (WMT 2014) it scored 28.4 BLEU. That beat the previous best results, including ensembles, by more than 2 BLEU.
  - On English-to-French it set a new single-model record of 41.8 BLEU. Training took 3.5 days on eight GPUs.
- **Generalization:** The model also worked well on English constituency parsing, with both large and limited training data. That suggests it isn't useful only for translation.

Here are three papers that together give a fair picture. I'm citing them from memory and haven't checked them against a live database, so confirm the details on PubMed before relying on them.

1. **Lowe DA et al. (2020), *JAMA Internal Medicine*. "Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity: The TREAT Randomized Clinical Trial."**
   - In this 12-week trial, 16:8 eating did not beat ordinary eating for weight loss.
   - A large share of the weight lost in the time-restricted group was lean mass, including appendicular lean mass.
   - It is often cited as the cautionary result for muscle loss. Caveats: the protein intake and resistance training were not controlled, and the sample was not made up of lifters.

2. **Moro T et al. (2016), *Journal of Translational Medicine*. "Effects of eight weeks of time-restricted feeding (16/8) on basal metabolism, maximal strength, body composition, inflammation, and cardiovascular risk factors in resistance-trained males."**
   - Resistance-trained men did 16:8 eating alongside their training.
   - They lost fat and kept their lean mass and strength.
   - It suggests that with resistance training and adequate protein, muscle can be preserved. The sample was small, though, and the trial was short.

3. **Cioffi I et al. (2018), *Journal of Translational Medicine*. "Intermittent versus continuous energy restriction on weight loss and cardiometabolic outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials."**
   - This pooled analysis compared intermittent and continuous calorie restriction.
   - Weight loss was similar for the two approaches, and fat-free mass changes were broadly comparable.
   - That points to total calorie deficit and protein intake, rather than the fasting pattern itself, as the main driver of muscle loss.

**Takeaway:** Intermittent fasting doesn't seem to cause extra muscle loss beyond what any calorie deficit causes. Muscle loss is more likely when protein is low and there is no resistance training. Most trials are short and small, so long-term evidence in older adults is thin.
